newsitem.title: FRANCE: French central bank head urges confidence in future.
newsitem.headline: French central bank head urges confidence in future.

text.p: Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said on Thursday the country's ailing economy was looking up and urged the French to be confident in the future.
"We have prospects for a rebound in European economic growth that are real," Trichet said in an interview on French television LCI. "We don't have the right to be so lacking in confidence."

Citing reports by various economic institutes, he said the French economy had "passed the trough", echoing a comment he made in London on Wednesday that stronger growth was clearly under way in France and the rest of Europe.

He said conditions were excellent for businesses to invest. "I tell them it's the moment to invest," he said. "You'll regret afterwards not having invested. You have exceptional financing conditions."
He would not comment directly on calls by former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing for a weaker currency to boost the economy but strongly defended France's strong monetary policy.

It had resulted in France having the third-lowest interest rates in the world, after Japan and Switzerland, thanks to the confidence of investors who were not necessarily "devoted francophiles", he said.

France's decade-old policy of keeping the franc steady against the powerful German mark was not penalising it in export terms, he added, as it boasted the world's third-largest trade surplus. "That proves the competitiveness," he said.
He said "a large majority of the French are attached" to having a currency that holds its value.
But while France was a prosperous country, it did have difficulty translating its wealth into job creation, he said, citing record 12.6 percent unemployment.
But France was not alone among European countries in having such a problem, he said, pointing to neighbouring countries where unemployment was also high.
While he said structural changes were needed to lower unemployment, he said he did not believe France could import job-creation solutions that went against its own social values.
